Supporting Information

Self-organizing dominance hierarchies generate the diversity of rank–stress profiles seen in social animals

Author

Simon D. W. Frost

Contents. Appendix S1: full model description (ODD protocol) and Table S1 (parameters). Appendix S2: verification (symbolic derivations, machine-checked proofs, automated tests). Appendix S3: supplementary results (Figures S1–S4). Appendix S4: group size and the contender contrast (Tables S4–S5).

Appendix S1. Full model description (ODD protocol)

This appendix describes the model as implemented, following the ODD protocol (Grimm et al. 2020). Unless stated otherwise, every quantity is dimensionless. Defaults are the values in the simulation code. The settings at the three base points used in the main text (A, B, C) and the values explored in each experiment are listed in Table S1. Notation: \(i\) is the focal individual (actor), \(j\) a partner (recipient) and \(k\) an asset; \(\sigma(x) = 1/(1+e^{-x})\); \((x)_+ = \max(x, 0)\).

1. Purpose and patterns

The model asks whether a near-transitive dominance hierarchy can emerge from local, experience-based decisions among initially identical individuals. Where one emerges, it asks which profiles of physiological burden across rank the same decisions generate. The model is built so that both the hierarchy and the burden are outputs. Individuals start exchangeable. Nobody is assigned a rank, and no behavioural or physiological parameter depends on status. Rank is computed only by the analyst, from the event log, after the run. It never enters any transition, belief, utility, policy or physiology equation. Load is never transmitted along network edges. An individual’s load changes only through the events it experiences and its own energy state.

The model is evaluated against three groups of patterns.

  1. Structure. The patterns are linear, near-linear, nontransitive, egalitarian, unstable and fragmented dominance structure, judged by triad transitivity, Landau’s \(h'\), observation coverage, persistence and held-out prediction.
  2. Rank–load profiles. The patterns reported in field studies are graded subordinate-high, dominant-high, U-shaped, inverted-U and flat profiles, with or without an exceptional alpha.
  3. Channels. The top-versus-bottom load gap is decomposed into its input channels (defeat, intimidation, effort, deficit, unpredictability).

2. Entities, state variables and scales

Individuals. There are \(N\) individuals (\(N = 10\) by default; 6–20 in the experiments). Each slot \(i\) carries the state variables below. Slot identifiers carry no strategic content: no agent uses them to choose.

Variable Domain Meaning
\(E_i\) \([0, 1]\) energy reserve
\(z_i\) \(\ge 0\) fast excess activation
\(A_i\) \(\ge 0\) slow allostatic load (recoverable burden)
\(B_i\) \(\ge 0\) received-support trace
\(R_i\) \([0, 1]\) functional reserve (only under coupling mechanism F4)
mode — forage, rest, withdrawn, holding a food patch, consorting
busy — none, fighting, grooming, cooperating (with partner and end time)
\(r_i\) \(\{0, 1\}\) mating readiness (1 for all individuals in season)
ledgers \(\ge 0\) cumulative intake, maintenance, effort, injury, waste and deficit \(D_i\)
beliefs — decaying evidence counts about each partner and pooled over partners (§7.4)
avoidance timers — time until which \(i\) avoids \(j\)
critic weights \(\mathbb{R}^7\) only under policy P4
subgroup \(\{1, \dots, n_{\mathrm{sub}}\}\) only under fission–fusion

The model also records counters for injuries, accepted matings and skipped opportunities, and the per-channel cumulative physiological inputs.

Assets. There are \(K_F\) food patches, each held by at most one individual. Optional mating seasons add \(K_M\) consortship assets, which exist only in season. Dispersed food is available everywhere and cannot be monopolized. Patch relocation is not implemented.

Environment and group. The model has no explicit space. Contact is a weighted sampling of the other group members at each decision opportunity (§7.2). Avoidance reduces the weights. Under fission–fusion, sampling is restricted to the individual’s current subgroup.

Scales. The time unit is the mean interval between one individual’s decision opportunities. Each individual’s opportunities follow a Poisson process of rate \(\nu = 1\), so total activity scales with \(N\), not \(N^2\). Runs last \(T_{\mathrm{run}} = 3000\) time units (\(9000\) at \(N = 20\)). Node states are recorded on a grid of spacing \(\Delta t_{\mathrm{rec}} = 1\). Physiological time scales are set relative to this unit: \(1/\lambda_z = 1\) for activation and \(1/\delta_{A0} = 100\) for load, so load integrates activation over about 100 decision intervals. Energy, activation, load and utility are dimensionless. Utility is measured in energy equivalents. Neither \(z\) nor \(A\) is a hormone concentration.

3. Process overview and scheduling

The model is a continuous-time discrete-event simulation. The event queue holds the following event types:

  • decision opportunities, a superposed Poisson process of rate \(N\nu\) with the actor drawn uniformly;
  • the scheduled ends of fights, grooming and cooperation;
  • mating attempts by idle consortship holders;
  • season boundaries;
  • random membership turnover and the optional targeted removal;
  • subgroup moves under fission–fusion;
  • recording-grid times.

Continuous state is advanced exactly and lazily, one individual at a time, only when that individual is touched by an event. The advanced state comprises energy, belief decay, the exposure times used by hazard beliefs, physiology and the reserve.

Decision opportunity. The random stream used at each step is given in brackets.

  1. Advance the actor to the current time. If it is busy, record a skipped opportunity and stop.
  2. Draw the encounter set and the visible assets [contact], and build the feasible option set (§7.2).
  3. Under P4 only, perform the actor’s temporal-difference update for the interval since its previous decision.
  4. Compute the value \(Q_i(d)\) of every feasible option. Under P4, add the learned continuation. Under P3D, add the deterrence value. Sample an option [choice].
  5. If the option is social, advance the recipient, compute its response values and sample a response [response].
  6. Resolve the interaction [contest]: the escape draw, or the fight outcome and injury.
  7. Apply the energy ledger (effort, escape and injury costs), asset transfers, mode changes and busy flags, and schedule the end of the interaction.
  8. Write exposure rows, apply physiological and support jumps, and update continuous inputs.
  9. Update the beliefs of the participants, and of bystanders if enabled. Set avoidance timers.
  10. Write the event row to the log.

All effects of an interaction are applied at the initiating event. The participants are then busy for the interaction’s duration (\(d_F\), \(d_G\) or \(d_C\)), and the scheduled end event only clears the busy flags and restores modes. An individual that still holds an asset resumes holding; every other participant enters forage mode.

Other events. Each first advances the affected individuals. A mating attempt draws acceptance [mating]. Season boundaries create or dissolve consortships. Turnover and removal replace an individual [shocks], and a subgroup move reassigns one [fission]. A grid time advances everyone and writes node rows.

4. Design concepts

Basic principles. The game combines four ideas: a finite energy budget with a solitary outside option (foraging alone); bounded-rational choice by expected subjective utility; Bayesian-style learning from one’s own experience; and a linear activation–load model of allostasis driven by an auditable ledger of realized events. The model keeps four levels separate: (a) objective ecological transitions and fitness proxies; (b) agents’ beliefs; (c) subjective utility; and (d) decision values and policies. The true win probability \(P_{ij}\), the agent’s forecast \(\hat p_{ij}\) and the analyst’s dominance estimate are distinct objects. Fitness proxies are recorded but never used for choice.

Emergence. The following are emergent: dominance structure; who holds patches and consortships; the network of directed outcomes, affiliation and avoidance; each individual’s exposure profile; and therefore the rank–load profile and its channel composition. None is imposed.

Adaptation. At each opportunity an individual chooses among feasible actions, targets and efforts by softmax over expected utility (§7.6). A recipient chooses its response in the same way. Choices depend on the individual’s energy (through the marginal value of energy), its holdings, the season and its beliefs.

Objectives. Each option is valued by the expected subjective utility of net energy, accepted matings, injuries, received safety events and received grooming, over a planning horizon \(H\) (§7.5). The baseline utility has no rank term and no load term.

Learning. Beliefs are decaying counts of the individual’s own experience (rate \(\gamma\)), turned into Beta and Dirichlet posterior means (§7.4). Under P4, each individual also learns a linear critic by semi-Markov TD(0) (Sutton and Barto 2018). No individual learns from another’s hidden state. Bystander learning, when enabled, uses only fights the bystander witnessed.

Prediction. Individuals forecast their win probability against each partner and the partner’s effort, response and acceptance. They also forecast the hazard of losing a held asset, the rates at which they are attacked, and the probability that a received attack ends badly. Under P3D an individual also predicts how a partner’s view of it, and hence the partner’s challenge rate, would change after the interaction. All predictions use only the individual’s own records.

Sensing. An individual observes its own energy, readiness, mode and holdings; the season calendar; which assets are held, by whom, and who is busy; its own encounters and the outcomes of its own interactions, including the partner’s effort after a fight; and, as structural knowledge, \(\phi\) and \(\phi_W\). It never observes another individual’s energy, activation, load, support or reserve, global rank, or any meaning in identifiers. Efforts are committed simultaneously, so a recipient does not see the actor’s effort when it responds.

Interaction. Interactions are direct and pairwise: challenges over held assets, aggression without a stake, grooming and cooperation. Positive interactions need the partner’s acceptance. Attacks do not, but the recipient may submit, attempt escape or fight. Indirect interaction comes through competition for a fixed number of patches and consortships, and through avoidance, which lowers contact rates after a defeat or yield.

Stochasticity. Ten independent random streams are each used only for their named purpose: schedule, contact, choice, response, contest, mating, learning, shocks, observation and fission. Stream seeds are derived from the run seed and stream name by SHA-256, so draws on one stream never shift another’s and results do not depend on parallel execution order. The learning stream is reserved (P4 updates are deterministic), and the observation stream serves only F1. Under common random numbers, replicate \(r\) of every point in a sweep uses the same seed.

Collectives. The group is the only collective, and the unit of replication. Fission–fusion subgroups (§7.9) restrict contact and do not make collective decisions.

Observation. All analysis is external to the simulation and follows frozen analysis plans; the main-text results use plan version 4. The event log records every proposal, response, contest, yield, affiliative event, exposure jump, mating attempt and membership change. Grid rows record each individual’s state and cumulative channel inputs.

  • Windows. After a burn-in of 1000, four windows of 500 are analysed. Each of the first three is classified, using the next window for persistence and held-out prediction. At \(N = 20\) the burn-in is 3000 and the windows are 1500 each.
  • Structure classes. Fights and yields are pooled as dominance evidence, and the first matching class is assigned:
    • fragmented: the contact graph is disconnected, or coverage \(< 0.6\);
    • Linear: \(h' \ge 0.8\), triangle transitivity above an orientation null (\(p < 0.05\)), coverage \(\ge 0.8\), and the held-out accuracy of a Bradley–Terry order at least that of dyad-specific majorities minus 0.02;
    • nontransitive: consistent dyads (DCI \(\ge 0.7\)), with transitivity not above the null or 3-cycles above it;
    • near-linear: transitive, consistent and persistent (rank persistence \(\ge 0.5\)), with \(h' \ge 0.6\);
    • egalitarian: DCI \(< 0.5\);
    • unstable: persistence \(< 0.5\).
  • Run class. The class shared by at least two of the three classified windows.
  • Ranks and profiles. Ranks are David’s scores. The rank–load profile rule is described in the main text.
  • Channel attribution. For the linear physiology, window-mean load decomposes exactly by input channel.

5. Initialization

All individuals start identical:

  • \(E_i = E_0 = 0.5\), \(z_i = 0\), \(A_i = \bar A = 0\), \(B_i = 0\) and \(R_i = 1\);
  • mode forage, holding nothing, not busy, with no avoidance;
  • every evidence count at zero, so every forecast is at its prior (§7.4);
  • under P4, critic weights at zero;
  • all patches free.

If \(K_M > 0\), the run starts at the beginning of a season. Under fission–fusion, initial subgroups are assigned uniformly [fission]. Under the controls, C1 status starts at 0 for all, and C3 draws its fixed dyadic win probabilities at \(t = 0\) [contest]. Every run writes a manifest with its seed lineage, configuration and software revision.

6. Input data

None. The model uses no external or empirical data, and no time series drives it.

7. Submodels

7.1 Ecology and energy ledger

Food. A forager takes in dispersed food at rate \(g_s\). A patch holder takes in \(g_P = \rho_c g_s\), with \(\rho_c \ge 1\). Scarcity is the ratio \(m/g_s\) of maintenance to dispersed intake: it is 0.8 at the defaults and 1.2 at base point A. With \(m/g_s > 1\) a lone forager loses energy. For matched-supply comparisons, total supply \(G_{\mathrm{tot}} = (N - K_F)g_s + K_F \rho_c g_s\) is held fixed and \(\rho_c\) is set from \(K_F\). This gives, for example, \(G_{\mathrm{tot}} = 0.475\) at \(N = 10\), so that \(K_F = 1\) gives \(\rho_c = 10\).

Modes. Intake \(g_\mu\) and expenditure \(m_\mu\) depend on the mode.

Mode Intake \(g_\mu\) Expenditure \(m_\mu\)
forage (fallback, outside option) \(g_s\) \(m\)
rest \(0\) \(m_{\mathrm{rest}}\)
withdrawn (refuge) \(\psi_W g_s\) \(m\)
holding a patch \(\rho_c g_s\) \(m\)
consorting \(\psi_M g_s\) \(m + m_G\)
busy: fight or grooming \(0\) \(m\)
busy: cooperation \((1+\sigma_c)g_s\), or \((1+\sigma_c)\rho_c g_s/2\) if either partner holds a patch \(m\)

Between events, \(\dot E_i = g_\mu - m_\mu\). Bounds are handled without clipping. The time at which \(E_i\) reaches 0 is computed in closed form and the interval is split there. At \(E_i = 0\) with \(g_\mu < m_\mu\), unpaid maintenance accrues as a recorded deficit, \(\dot D_i = m_\mu - g_\mu\). At \(E_i = 1\), excess intake is recorded as waste. Instantaneous costs are charged at the event:

  • effort \(c_e e\) to each fighter;
  • \(c_{\mathrm{esc}}\) per escape attempt;
  • \(E_{\mathrm{inj}}\) per injury.

Any part of a cost exceeding \(E_i\) is added to \(D_i\). After every event the simulator checks the conservation identity \[E_i(t) = E_i(0) + \mathrm{Intake}_i - \mathrm{Basal}_i - \mathrm{Effort}_i - \mathrm{Injury}_i - \mathrm{Waste}_i + D_i.\] Time costs enter only as forgone intake.

Fitness proxies. These are recorded only and never used for choice. The survival proxy is \(-\ln S_i = \mu_0 t + \mu_D T^{E=0}_i + \mu_I n^{\mathrm{inj}}_i\), where \(T^{E=0}_i\) is the time spent in deficit. The model also records the number of accepted matings \(M_i\).

7.2 Actions, responses and outcomes

Contact. At an opportunity, the actor samples up to \(n_{\mathrm{enc}} = 2\) encountered individuals from those not busy [contact]:

  1. Each withdrawn candidate is protected, and excluded, with probability \(\phi_W\).
  2. Each remaining candidate has weight \(1 - v\) if either individual avoids the other (an avoider holding a patch does not avoid), and weight 1 otherwise.
  3. Candidates are drawn by weighted sampling without replacement (Efraimidis–Spirakis keys).

The actor also sees up to \(n_{\mathrm{vis}} = 2\) assets, drawn uniformly from the existing assets other than its own, together with their occupancy and holders.

Initiator actions. Effort is discrete, \(e \in \{e_L, e_H\}\), and is chosen before the outcome.

  • FORAGE, REST: always feasible.
  • WITHDRAW: feasible when \(\phi_W > 0\).
  • KEEP: continue holding the current asset.
  • OCCUPY\((k)\): take a visible free asset.
  • CHALLENGE\((j, k, e)\): contest the holder \(j\) of a visible asset \(k\), provided \(j\) is not busy.
  • AGGRESS\((j, e)\): attack an encountered individual without a stake.
  • AFFILIATE\((j)\): propose grooming.
  • COOPERATE\((j)\): propose joint foraging or patch sharing. Feasible only if neither partner is consorting and at most one holds a patch.

Holder rules:

  • An individual holds at most one asset. OCCUPY and CHALLENGE are feasible only for non-holders.
  • Choosing FORAGE, REST or WITHDRAW releases the held asset.
  • A holder keeps its asset during AGGRESS, grooming and cooperation, and cannot be challenged while busy.
  • Consortships can be occupied or challenged only in season.

Responses.

  • To CHALLENGE or AGGRESS: SUBMIT, ESCAPE, or FIGHT with effort \(e_L\) or \(e_H\).
  • To AFFILIATE: ACCEPT, RECIPROCATE (grooming in both directions) or DECLINE.
  • To COOPERATE: ACCEPT or DECLINE.

A declined proposal costs the proposer only the opportunity.

Outcomes.

  • SUBMIT. To a CHALLENGE, the stake passes to the actor and the recipient enters forage mode. To an AGGRESS, the recipient keeps its mode.
  • ESCAPE. The recipient pays \(c_{\mathrm{esc}}\) and succeeds with probability \(\phi\) [contest]. Escape has no duration. Under a CHALLENGE the stake is ceded whether or not escape succeeds. A failed escape counts as a yield that also received the attack.
  • FIGHT. Both pay \(c_e e\) and are busy for \(d_F\). The winner keeps or takes the stake. The loser is injured with probability \(\iota\, e_{\mathrm{winner}}\), paying \(E_{\mathrm{inj}}\).
  • Accepted grooming. Both are busy for \(d_G\) with no intake.
  • Accepted cooperation. Both are busy for \(d_C\) at the cooperative intake rate.

Avoidance. This is a fixed rule, not a choice. After losing a fight to \(j\), submitting to \(j\) or attempting escape from \(j\), individual \(i\) avoids \(j\) for \(\tau_V\). Avoidance lowers the contact weight between the pair (above).

7.3 Contest success function

The objective probability that \(i\) beats \(j\) is a Tullock contest success function (Skaperdas 1996) with condition dependence: \[P_{ij} = \frac{c_i e_i^{\theta}}{c_i e_i^{\theta} + c_j e_j^{\theta}} = \sigma\!\left(\theta \ln\frac{e_i}{e_j} + \zeta \ln\frac{\varepsilon_c + E_i}{\varepsilon_c + E_j}\right), \qquad c_i = (\varepsilon_c + E_i)^{\zeta}.\] Here \(\theta\) is decisiveness and \(\zeta\) is condition dependence; \(P_{ij} + P_{ji} = 1\). The outcome is drawn on the contest stream. The function provides two separately testable routes to order:

  • Belief route (\(\zeta = 0\)). Outcomes are effort lotteries, and any structure must come from partner-specific beliefs and choices.
  • Resource-holding route (\(\zeta > 0\)). Winning patches raises \(E\), and higher \(E\) raises later win probability. Because \(E_i\) is a per-individual scalar, this route favours transitivity. It is earned through ecology, not assigned.

Agents never observe \(E_j\), so the condition term never enters their forecasts.

Controls. These replace the primary contest function in comparison arms.

  • C1, scalar winner–loser comparator. \(P_{ij} = \sigma(\beta_s(s_i - s_j) + \theta\ln(e_i/e_j))\), with status updates \(s_w \mathrel{+}= \Delta(1 - P)\) and \(s_l \mathrel{-}= \Delta(1 - P)\), where \(P\) is the winner’s pre-fight win probability. It is transitive by construction.
  • C3, fixed random dyadic. \(\mathrm{logit}\,P_{ij} = \mathrm{logit}\,U_{ij} + \theta\ln(e_i/e_j)\), with \(U_{ij} \sim \mathrm{U}(0,1)\) drawn once and \(U_{ji} = 1 - U_{ij}\).

7.4 Beliefs

Evidence counts. Each individual \(i\) holds counts about each partner \(j\), built from its own experience:

  • fight wins \(w_{ij}\) and losses \(l_{ij}\), in either role;
  • yields received \(s^+_{ij}\) (\(j\) submitted to or attempted escape from \(i\)) and yields given \(s^-_{ij}\);
  • \(j\)’s high-effort and low-effort uses against \(i\);
  • \(j\)’s responses (submit, escape, fight) to \(i\)’s challenges and, separately, to \(i\)’s aggression;
  • acceptances and declines of \(i\)’s grooming and cooperation proposals, and reciprocation given acceptance.

Pooled counts over all partners give \(i\)’s own baseline frequencies. They also record challenges received, assets lost and decayed holding time (separately for patches and consortships); aggression received and decayed time while not holding; received attacks and those that ended badly; and own mating attempts accepted and rejected. All counts decay as \(e^{-\gamma\Delta t}\), applied lazily on read. Direct dominance evidence is \(n_{ij} = w_{ij} + l_{ij} + s^+_{ij} + s^-_{ij}\). A dyad with \(n_{ij} < n_U\) is unobserved, which is not the same as an observed equal relationship. Pooled frequencies use uniform priors, \((1 + x)/(K + \textstyle\sum)\) for \(K\) categories, so they equal \(1/K\) with no experience.

Win forecast. A Beta posterior mean: \[\hat p_{ij} = \frac{a_i + w_{ij} + \omega_S s^+_{ij} + w^{\mathrm{obs}}_{ij}}{2\alpha + w_{ij} + l_{ij} + \omega_S(s^+_{ij} + s^-_{ij}) + w^{\mathrm{obs}}_{ij} + l^{\mathrm{obs}}_{ij}}.\] Here \(a_i = \alpha\) by default. The effort-conditional forecast is \(\hat p_{ij}(e, \hat e_j) = \sigma(\mathrm{logit}\,\hat p_{ij} + \beta_{\mathrm{opt}} + \theta\ln(e/\hat e_j))\), which assumes that agents know effort matters. The optimism bias \(\beta_{\mathrm{opt}}\) is 0 by default.

Other forecasts.

  • Effort. \(\hat\pi^H_{ij} = (\alpha \bar f^H_i + f^H_{ij})/(\alpha + f^H_{ij} + f^L_{ij})\), where \(\bar f^H_i\) is \(i\)’s pooled high-effort frequency across opponents. Then \(\hat e_j = e_L + \hat\pi^H_{ij}(e_H - e_L)\) is used as a point estimate.
  • Responses. For each context (stake or no stake), the Dirichlet posterior mean \(\hat\pi_{ij} = (\alpha_R \bar R_i + R_{ij})/(\alpha_R + \sum R_{ij})\), where \(\bar R_i\) is \(i\)’s pooled response frequency and \(\alpha_R = 3\).
  • Acceptance and reciprocation. \(\hat a_{ij} = (2\bar a_i + Y_{ij})/(2 + Y_{ij} + N_{ij})\), where \(\bar a_i\) is \(i\)’s pooled acceptance frequency.
  • Mate acceptance. \(\hat a_i = (1 + Y^{\mathrm{mate}}_i)/(2 + Y^{\mathrm{mate}}_i + N^{\mathrm{mate}}_i)\).
  • Holding hazard, by asset type \(\tau\): a Gamma–Beta estimate, \[\hat h_i(\tau) = \frac{a_h + n^{\mathrm{ch}}_i(\tau)}{b_h + T^{\mathrm{hold}}_i(\tau)} \cdot \frac{\alpha + n^{\mathrm{lost}}_i(\tau)}{2\alpha + n^{\mathrm{ch}}_i(\tau)}.\] The first factor is the perceived attack rate while holding, \(\hat\lambda_i(\tau)\).
  • Attack rate while free. \(\hat\lambda_i(\varnothing) = (a_h + n^{\mathrm{agg}}_i)/(b_h + T^{\mathrm{free}}_i)\), counting aggression received while foraging or resting.
  • Expected safety cost per received attack. \(\varsigma_i = s_S(\alpha + n^{\mathrm{bad}}_i)/(2\alpha + n^{\mathrm{att}}_i)\).

Exposure times accrue only while the individual is not busy.

Optional mechanisms coupling beliefs across dyads. These are off by default and are ablated separately.

  • Standing cue. \(\hat s_i = (1 + W_i)/(2 + W_i + L_i)\), where \(W_i\) is \(i\)’s decayed number of fights won plus yields received over all partners, and \(L_i\) is fights lost plus yields given. With the cue on, the prior for every partner becomes \(\mathrm{Beta}(2\alpha\hat s_i, 2\alpha(1 - \hat s_i))\), that is, \(a_i = 2\alpha\hat s_i\). The prior strength is unchanged.
  • Bystander learning. Bystanders of a fight are the other members of the actor’s encounter set. A bystander adds a pseudo-loss of weight \(\omega_{\mathrm{obs}}\) to its record against the winner and a pseudo-win against the loser. Pseudo-counts (\(w^{\mathrm{obs}}\), \(l^{\mathrm{obs}}\)) enter \(\hat p\) but not \(n_{ij}\), so observation never makes a dyad directly observed.

Learning controls. C2 freezes every count at its prior. P2-pooled freezes the partner-specific counts but still learns the pooled ones.

7.5 Utilities and decision values

Utility. Energy is valued by a concave, state-dependent function, \(\Phi(E) = E_h(1 - e^{-E/E_h})\), so \(\Phi'(E) = e^{-E/E_h}\): an energy change is worth more to a hungry individual. The utility of an outcome \(o\) is \[u_i(o) = \Phi'(E_i)\,\Delta E_i(o) + s^u_M r_i\, n^{\mathrm{mate}}_i(o) - s_H\, n^{\mathrm{inj}}_i(o) - s_S\, n^{\mathrm{saf}}_i(o) + s_G\, n^{\mathrm{aff}}_i(o).\]

  • \(\Delta E\) is net energy. It already includes effort, forgone intake and injury energy, and at decision time it is the unclipped linear prediction.
  • Safety events are received attacks that end badly for the recipient: a submission, a failed escape or a fight defeat.
  • \(n^{\mathrm{aff}}\) counts received grooming only. Received cooperation is valued through \(\Delta E\), to avoid double counting.
  • The subjective safety cost \(s_S\) is an aversion valued at decision time. It does not read \(z\) or \(A\).

Value components. All values are measured relative to remaining in forage mode, the outside option.

  • Horizon factor. \(\Lambda(h; H) = (1 - e^{-(\kappa + h)H})/(\kappa + h)\), with \(\Lambda_0 = \Lambda(0; H)\).
  • Asset value. \(W_i(k) = \upsilon_i(k)\,\Lambda(\hat h_i(\tau_k); H_k)\). For a patch, \(\upsilon = \Phi'(E_i)(\hat\rho_c - 1)g_s - \varsigma_i(\hat\lambda_i(F) - \hat\lambda_i(\varnothing))\), where \(\hat\rho_c = \rho_c\) unless a misperceived richness is set (Table S1). For a consortship, \(\upsilon = \Phi'(E_i)(\psi_M g_s - m_G - g_s) + s^u_M\mu_m\hat a_i - \varsigma_i(\hat\lambda_i(M) - \hat\lambda_i(\varnothing))\). The horizon is \(H_k = H\) for patches and \(\min(H, t^{\mathrm{end}}_{\mathrm{season}} - t)\) for consortships.
  • Forgone flow while busy. \(\ell_i = \Phi'(E_i)g_{\mathrm{cur},i} + s^u_M\mu_m\hat a_i\mathbf{1}[i\ \mathrm{consorting}]\).
  • Expected fight cost. \[K_i(e; j) = \ell_i d_F + \Phi'(E_i)c_e e + \big(1 - \hat p_{ij}(e, \hat e_j)\big)\big[s_S + \iota\hat e_j(s_H + \Phi'(E_i)E_{\mathrm{inj}})\big].\]
  • Current holding term. \(\mathcal{H}_i = W_i(k_i)\) if \(i\) holds \(k_i\), and 0 otherwise.

Initiator values.

Option \(Q_i(d)\)
FORAGE \(0\)
REST \(\Phi'(E_i)(m - m_{\mathrm{rest}} - g_s)\Lambda_0\)
WITHDRAW \(\big[\Phi'(E_i)(\psi_W - 1)g_s + \varsigma_i\phi_W\hat\lambda_i(\varnothing)\big]\Lambda_0\)
KEEP, OCCUPY\((k)\) \(W_i(k)\)
CHALLENGE\((j,k,e)\) \((\hat\pi^{\mathrm{sub}}_{ij} + \hat\pi^{\mathrm{esc}}_{ij})W_i(k) + \hat\pi^{\mathrm{fight}}_{ij}\big[\hat p_{ij}(e,\hat e_j)W_i(k) - K_i(e;j)\big]\)
AGGRESS\((j,e)\) \(\mathcal{H}_i - \hat\pi^{\mathrm{fight}}_{ij}K_i(e;j)\) (no-stake response forecast)
AFFILIATE\((j)\) \(\mathcal{H}_i + \hat a^G_{ij}\big[s_G\hat\rho^{\mathrm{rec}}_{ij} - \ell_i d_G\big]\)
COOPERATE\((j)\) \(\mathcal{H}_i + \hat a^C_{ij}d_C\big[\Phi'(E_i)g^C_{ij} - \ell_i\big]\)

Here \(g^C_{ij}\) is the cooperative intake of §7.1.

Recipient values. These are relative to the recipient’s status quo, with stake value \(W = W_j(k)\) for a CHALLENGE and \(W = 0\) for an AGGRESS: \[Q_j(\mathrm{SUBMIT}) = -W - s_S, \qquad Q_j(\mathrm{ESCAPE}) = -W - \Phi'(E_j)c_{\mathrm{esc}} - (1-\phi)s_S,\] \[Q_j(\mathrm{FIGHT}(e')) = -\big(1 - \hat p_{ji}(e', \hat e_i)\big)W - K_j(e'; i).\] For grooming, \(Q_j(\mathrm{ACCEPT}) = Q_j(\mathrm{RECIPROCATE}) = s_G - \ell_j d_G\). For cooperation, \(Q_j(\mathrm{ACCEPT}) = d_C[\Phi'(E_j)g^C_{ji} - \ell_j]\). Declining is worth 0.

Consequently, ESCAPE beats SUBMIT exactly when \(\phi s_S > \Phi'(E_j)c_{\mathrm{esc}}\); AGGRESS has no positive immediate value, so myopic policies choose it only through noise; and at \(s_G = 0\) grooming has negative immediate value.

7.6 Policies

P2 (primary; myopic softmax). The option is chosen with probability \[\pi_i(d) = \frac{\exp(Q_i(d)/T)}{\sum_{d' \in \mathcal{D}_i}\exp(Q_i(d')/T)}, \qquad T = \tau_T U_{\mathrm{ref}}, \quad U_{\mathrm{ref}} = \Phi'(E_0)g_s H.\] The choice is over the enumerated (action, target, effort) options, with \(H = 10\). Responses use the same rule. Tying the temperature to the reference utility makes \(\tau_T\) a relative noise level. Softmax over enumerated options weights action types by their number of targets and efforts. This weighting is declared, not corrected. Softmax convergence is not a Nash equilibrium.

P3 and P3-T (long horizon). P3 is P2 with \(H = 100\). Because \(T\) scales with \(H\), P3 also changes the absolute noise. P3-T evaluates values at \(H = 100\) but keeps the temperature scale at \(H = 10\) (\(T_H = 10\)).

P4 (learned continuation). The value of an option is \[Q_i(d) = Q^{\mathrm{imm}}_i(d) + e^{-\kappa/\nu}\sum_b \hat\pi_b \hat V_i(x'_b).\]

  • \(Q^{\mathrm{imm}}\) is the P2 value computed with the immediate horizon \(H_{\mathrm{imm}} = 1\).
  • The branches \(b\) are weighted by \(i\)’s own response and win forecasts.
  • In the predicted post-outcome states \(x'_b\) only holdings and the standing \(\hat s_i\) change (by one win or one loss). Energy is not projected.
  • The critic is linear, \(\hat V_i = w_i\cdot\varphi\), with features \(\varphi\) = (1, \(E_i\), holds a patch, holds a consortship, \(\hat s_i\), in season). Variant P4b adds \(i\)’s mean win forecast over all others.
  • Learning. At each of \(i\)’s non-skipped opportunities the critic takes a semi-Markov TD(0) step (Sutton and Barto 2018). With \(s_n\) the state at the previous opportunity and \(s_{n+1}\) the current one, \(\delta = R + e^{-\kappa\Delta t}\hat V(s_{n+1}) - \hat V(s_n)\) and \(w \leftarrow w + \alpha_w\delta\varphi(s_n)/\lVert\varphi(s_n)\rVert^2\).
  • Reward. \(R\) is the exact change \(\Phi(E_{t_{n+1}}) - \Phi(E_{t_n})\) plus non-energy utility accrued in the interval: \(-s_S\) per safety event, \(-s_H\) per injury, \(+s^u_M\) per accepted mating and \(+s_G\) per grooming received, including events the individual did not choose.
  • No actor update. P4 is a learned critic combined with softmax choice at the P2 temperature. With \(\alpha_w = 0\) and \(H_{\mathrm{imm}} = H\) it reproduces P2 exactly.

P3D (deterrence-aware planning). This is P3-T plus a deterrence value on contest options and on responses to attacks.

  • Individual \(i\) estimates \(j\)’s forecast against it by reading its own record about \(j\) from \(j\)’s side: \(\tilde p_{ji} = (\alpha + l_{ij} + \omega_S s^-_{ij})/(2\alpha + w_{ij} + l_{ij} + \omega_S(s^+_{ij} + s^-_{ij}))\).
  • It models \(j\)’s challenge rate on its holdings as \(\lambda_j = 2\tilde p_{ji}\hat h_i/(N - 1)\).
  • For each outcome \(o\) (j yields, \(i\) wins, \(i\) loses, \(i\) yields), \(D(o) = -[\lambda'_j(o) - \lambda_j]H_d(1 - \hat p_{ij})W_i\), with \(H_d = (1 - e^{-(\kappa+\gamma)H})/(\kappa+\gamma)\).
  • \(Q\) gains \(\sum_o \hat\pi(o)D(o)\).

All of these inputs come from the individual’s own records.

Reference policies. These are used only in comparison arms.

  • P0. Uniform over feasible action types, then over targets and efforts.
  • P1. Fixed hawk, dove or bourgeois rules.
  • C2. No learning.

7.7 Exposure ledger

Physiological inputs come only from realized events and states. Every jump is a row of an auditable ledger with its time, individual, channel, magnitude and buffer factor. Continuous inputs are kept as exact cumulative totals. No rank appears in any row.

Channel Trigger Form Magnitude Pathway
defeat lose a fight (either role) jump \(q_D\) threat
intimidation yield: SUBMIT or failed ESCAPE, to CHALLENGE or AGGRESS jump \(q_S\) threat
injury injured in a fight jump \(q_I\) threat
unpredictability fight lost, injury or failed escape, scored against the individual’s own forecast jump \(\beta_U[-\ln\hat p(\mathrm{outcome})]\) threat
contest effort take part in a fight, win or lose, with own effort \(e\) jump \(q_E e\) effort
escape effort escape attempt, success or failure jump \(q_{\mathrm{esc}}\) effort
activity forage, withdrawn, holding, consorting, cooperating continuous \(\beta_W(m - m_{\mathrm{rest}})\) effort
guarding consorting continuous \(\beta_W m_G\) effort
deficit \(E_i = 0\) with deficit accruing continuous \(\beta_D\) deprivation
anticipatory threat holding an asset (off by default) continuous \(\beta_T\max(\hat h_i W_i, 0)/U_{\mathrm{ref}}\) threat

Accounting rules.

  • A fight gives one contest-effort jump to each participant and one defeat jump to the loser. The activity input is zero during fights and grooming, so no continuous term duplicates a fight’s jumps.
  • Each yield gives exactly one intimidation jump. A successful escape gives escape effort only.
  • Effort inputs apply to winners as well (the cost-of-dominance pathway).
  • Unpredictability is scored against the experiencing individual’s own forecast at commitment:
    • a lost fight, \(1 - \hat p_{ij}(e_i, \hat e_j)\);
    • an injury, \(\iota\hat e_j\);
    • a failed escape, \(1 - \phi\).
  • Fight and injury surprise apply only when the loser’s direct evidence about the winner was at least \(n_U\) before the fight.
  • Positive outcomes, chosen submissions, declined proposals, rejected matings and season-end losses are not scored.
  • Threat-pathway inputs are multiplied by the support buffer \(\beta_B(B_i)\) (§7.8). Effort and deficit inputs never are.
  • The safety term \(s_S\) of §7.5 is a separate, decision-time aversion and is not a physiological input.

7.8 Physiology

Activation and load follow \[\dot z_i = -\lambda_z z_i + u_i(t), \qquad \dot A_i = k z_i^{p} - \delta_A(B_i)(A_i - \bar A),\] with jumps at events, \[z_i(t^+) = z_i(t^-) + \beta_B(B_i)\,q^{\mathrm{threat}} + q^{\mathrm{effort}}, \qquad u_i = \beta_B(B_i)u_T + u_W + u_D.\] The defaults are \(p = 1\), \(\lambda_z = 1 \gg \delta_{A0} = 0.01\), \(\bar A = 0\), and \(k = \lambda_z\delta_{A0}\). This choice of \(k\) makes the stationary mean excess load equal to the mean input rate. The support trace decays, \(\dot B_i = -\lambda_B B_i\). It jumps by \(b_G\) when \(i\) receives grooming and by \(b_C\) for each cooperation partner, applied at acceptance.

Support. The two mechanisms are tested separately, and neither subtracts load directly.

  • Threat buffering: \(\beta_B(B) = 1 - \eta_B B/(K_B + B)\) scales threat inputs only.
  • Recovery facilitation: \(\delta_A(B) = \delta_{A0}[1 + \rho_B B/(K_B + B)]\).

Integration.

  • Exact engine (\(p = 1\), \(\rho_B = 0\), piecewise-constant input). Between events the closed-form flow map is used: \[z(\tau) = z_0 e^{-\lambda_z\tau} + \frac{u}{\lambda_z}(1 - e^{-\lambda_z\tau}),\] \[A(\tau) = \bar A + (A_0 - \bar A)e^{-\delta_A\tau} + k z_0\frac{e^{-\delta_A\tau} - e^{-\lambda_z\tau}}{\lambda_z - \delta_A} + \frac{ku}{\lambda_z}\left[\frac{1 - e^{-\delta_A\tau}}{\delta_A} - \frac{e^{-\delta_A\tau} - e^{-\lambda_z\tau}}{\lambda_z - \delta_A}\right].\] These expressions and the window integrals of \(z\) and \(A\) are evaluated as divided differences of the exponential. Every coefficient is then positive, so \(z, A \ge 0\) hold in floating point without clipping, and the equal-rate limit needs no separate branch. Intervals are split where \(E\) reaches 0, so the deficit input starts exactly.
  • Semi-analytic engine (\(p \ne 1\), \(\rho_B > 0\), or buffering acting on a nonzero \(u_T\)). \(z\) is in closed form, and \(A\) is computed from its convolution form by adaptive quadrature at relative tolerance physio_rtol. The integral of \(\delta_A(B(s))\) is in closed form.

Analytic properties. These were verified symbolically and, where stated in the main text, by machine-checked proof:

  • with zero input, \(z \to 0\) and \(A \to \bar A\);
  • under constant input, \(z^* = u/\lambda_z\) and \(A^* = \bar A + (k/\delta_A)(u/\lambda_z)^p\);
  • a single pulse \(q\) gives \(A(t) - \bar A = kq(e^{-\delta_A t} - e^{-\lambda_z t})/(\lambda_z - \delta_A)\);
  • jumps at mean rate \(r\) give mean excess load \(krq/(\lambda_z\delta_A)\), independent of their temporal clustering in the linear model.

An independent ODE solver with jump callbacks is used in tests only.

7.9 Optional mechanisms

Mating seasons and consortships (off by default, \(K_M = 0\)).

  • Each period of length \(T_{\mathrm{season}}\) starts with an in-season interval of length \(s_M T_{\mathrm{season}}\). During it there are \(K_M\) consortship assets and \(r_i = 1\) for every individual. With \(s_M = 1\) the breeding position is year-round.
  • An idle consort makes mating attempts as a Poisson process of rate \(\mu_m\) [mating], paused while it is busy. Each attempt is accepted with probability \(a\) (default 0.5), independently of contest history. Optionally, \(a_i = \sigma(\mathrm{logit}\,a + \chi(x_i - \tfrac12))\), with \(x_i\) the objective decayed fight-win share.
  • Consorting costs an extra \(m_G\) (guarding) and reduces intake to \(\psi_M g_s\).
  • At season end all consortships dissolve and their holders enter forage mode.

Fission–fusion (off by default, \(n_{\mathrm{sub}} = 1\)).

  • There are \(n_{\mathrm{sub}}\) subgroups. Each individual moves at rate \(\omega_{FF}\) to a uniformly chosen subgroup, possibly its own [fission].
  • Encounters are restricted to co-present individuals. Visible assets are free assets and assets held by co-present individuals.
  • Holdings, ongoing interactions and mating are unaffected by moves.

Membership turnover and targeted removal.

  • Random turnover. At group rate \(\xi\) [shocks], a uniformly chosen individual is replaced by a naive newcomer. The newcomer gets the initial state, the prior beliefs and, under P4, zero critic weights. Every other individual’s records about that slot are erased. Any asset it held becomes free, and an ongoing interaction ends for its partner.
  • Targeted removal. This is a declared experimenter intervention. At removal_time, the individual with the highest David’s score is replaced in the same way. The score is computed analyst-side from the dominance records of the preceding 500 time units, and ties are broken on the shocks stream. It is not an agent rule, and the score it uses enters no behavioural, belief or physiological equation.

Two-way coupling (off by default; enabled one at a time). With all four mechanisms off, coupling is one-way: load cannot affect choices, effort or contest outcomes.

  • F1, private burden cost (P4 only). At each TD step, \(R \mathrel{-}= w_A\tilde a\). Here \(\tilde a = \left(\int z\,dt\right)\exp(\sigma_a\epsilon - \sigma_a^2/2)\), the integral is taken over the inter-decision interval, and \(\epsilon \sim N(0,1)\) is drawn on the observation stream. F1 has no channel into P2 or P3.
  • F2, load-limited effort capacity. The feasible high effort is \(e_L + (e_H - e_L)(1 - (A_i - \bar A)/A_{\mathrm{cap}})_+\), evaluated at decision or response time. The high option is dropped when it equals \(e_L\). This is a capacity limit, not a sensed signal.
  • F3, load-slowed recovery. \(\delta_A(A, B) = \delta_A(B)/(1 + \chi_A(A - \bar A))\), integrated by adaptive Dormand–Prince 5(4), with \(z\) and \(B\) in closed form. This is the only mechanism under which temporal clustering of inputs can change mean load. The channel decomposition does not hold under F3.
  • F4, functional reserve. The reserve follows \[\dot R_i = \frac{\rho_R(1 - R_i)}{1 + \chi_R(A_i - \bar A)} - \eta_R R_i\frac{z_i^{m}}{K_z^{m} + z_i^{m}}, \qquad R_i(0) = 1,\] and \(R_i \in [0, 1]\) is proved invariant. It caps the feasible high effort at \(e_L + (e_H - e_L)R_i\). If F2 is also set, F4 takes precedence.

Automated tests (Julia). 13,744 tests in eleven groups: random-stream independence and reproducibility; package quality (Aqua); agreement with the generated symbolic references; physiology (analytic tests and comparison with an independent ODE solver with jump callbacks); the game (ledger identity after every event, feasibility, invariants, controls); exposure (exact decomposition of load into channels, and a test that load never reaches decisions under one-way coupling); structure analysis; rank–load and profile-shape rules; two-way coupling; sensitivity estimators; and the stage-game benchmark.

Appendix S3. Supplementary results

Appendix S4. Group size and the contender contrast

Design. The shape results in the main text come from groups of 6 and 10. Closed groups of 20 do not order at base A, so the \(N = 20\) tests used the settings known to order at that size: fast fission–fusion (four subgroups, move rate 0.03) for the base-A scenarios, with matched \(N = 10\) fission–fusion controls, and bases B and C. Predictions were fixed before the runs. Windows were three times longer at \(N = 20\) (burn-in 3,000, windows of 1,500), and each cell had 40 groups.

L1 / F0 base A + FF 20 / 10 40 / 35 subordinate-high, graded / same subordinate-high: holds

L3 base B 20 0 – untestable

L6 / F5 mating monopoly + FF 20 / 10 9 / 31 subordinate-high, alpha trough / same subordinate-high, no alpha peak: holds

Re-running the earlier \(N = 20\) designs to add profile records reproduced every previously recorded output bit for bit. In those designs, every setting without scarcity that ordered at least 12 of 20 groups had its mean profile peak at rank 2 or 3, above a flat remainder and below a low-load alpha. The thirds rule read these profiles as dominant-high or, once, as flat, because at \(N = 20\) ranks 2–3 lie inside the top third with the alpha.

Contender contrast. To describe this profile at any group size we defined, after the scan and before a confirmation run on new seeds (K14, K18), the contender contrast \[\kappa = \tfrac12\left(\ell_{(2)} + \ell_{(3)}\right) - \operatorname{mean}\left(\ell_{(5)}, \dots, \ell_{(N)}\right),\] on the same standardized, score-ordered profile as the shape rule. Position 4 is excluded as a buffer. The confirmation prediction was \(\ge 5\) ordered groups, a \(\kappa\) interval above 0.5 and an alpha trough, in both cells. It held.

At the 31 base-B scan points with at least 5 ordered groups (post hoc), \(\kappa\) exceeded 0.9 at all 19 points with three patches of richness \(\rho_c \ge 4\). These include the channel ablations, support and coupling variants of that cell. \(\kappa\) was at most 0.57 at the 12 points with poor patches (\(\rho_c \le 2\)) or in the matched-supply design of patch number and escape. The contender peak therefore requires several rich, contestable patches without scarcity.
